visible.summary: Comoros is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code criminalises acts “contrary to morality or against nature” (2 years), enforced: two women were detained in June 2024 after asking an Islamic preacher to marry them, convicted in December 2024 (released for time served). No LGR; small conservative archipelago.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2020 criminalisation and the 2024 prosecution show active enforcement of morality provisions — trans visitors are captured via birth-sex status; the case also signals risk for anyone in a same-sex relationship.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: 2024 prosecution is same-sex (climate); shows active enforcement.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents that Comoros criminalises same-sex sexual activity (up to 3 years' imprisonment under the penal code).
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Dec 2024) covers a couple in Comoros released after a same-sex sentencing verdict.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report (Comoros): same-sex conduct criminalised under the penal code, but authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions during 2023 and did not actively enforce the law; no non-discrimination law; police reported not to incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons and none was reported that year; widespread impunity listed among major human-rights problems. (Corrects the old claim: the Dec 2024 couple conviction is not in this 2023 report — it comes from the 2024 Outright/Blade sources.)

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Comoros: general human-rights baseline (poor prisons, restrictions on movement/press/religion, discrimination against women) with limited LGBT-specific content.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Art. 300 of the 2020 penal code punishes same-sex acts with 6 months–2 years plus a 100,000–300,000 franc (US$240–720) fine; no discrimination protections, no legal gender-marker change, no known LGBTIQ organisations (Art. 5 of Law 86-006/AF chills registration); enforcement documented — first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy after a leaked video (2022), first same-sex arrests of two women June 2024, conviction Dec 2024 with time served; government repeatedly refused UN decriminalisation recommendations.

Washington Blade (23 Dec 2024): Comoros court on 12 Dec 2024 sentenced two lesbian women to five and six months for homosexuality and released them with time served — the couple had been arrested in June 2024 after asking an imam to marry them; first conviction of this kind, called a human-rights violation by Human Dignity Trust; article cites Art. 318 (up to five years) as the provision.

visible.summary: Djibouti is dangerous for trans visitors. The penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct, but vague “good morals” provisions (Arts 353/354) make homosexuality “de facto illegal” in practice; no anti-discrimination law, no LGR, no community infrastructure; authoritarian state with US/French bases but no rights space.
visible.tangentialFactors: The "good morals" provisions de facto criminalise homosexuality — trans visitors are captured via birth-sex status and presentation.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): penal code §§ 353–354 refer vaguely to 'good morals' with no explicit criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, yet their at-a-glance table still marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country; no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register; current-fact: still no explicit offence, but 'obscene acts'/public morality provisions are used against people.

Wikipedia overview (current): legality of same-sex conduct is ambiguous — no law says either way, but authorities can prosecute public same-sex conduct under 'good morals' provisions, so it is treated as de facto illegal; discrimination protection exists in employment only; no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report, Djibouti SOGIESC section: law does not explicitly criminalise consensual LGBTQI+ conduct, but status and conduct are taboo; a societal pattern of discrimination with no official violence cases citable — complaints can be filed with police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH); no legal prohibition of SOGI discrimination; pervasive social and religious intolerance makes people fear family and community shunning on disclosure.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Djibouti: general human-rights assessment (suppression of opposition, harsh prisons, FGM, trafficking) - baseline context with limited LGBT-specific content.

Canadian IRB Response to Information Request DJI104070.E (research 2009–Mar 2012, via ecoi.net): documentation on treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti was scarce across all consulted sources, leaning on the US 2010 country report — a dated historical baseline showing how little legal/protection framework and support services existed in that period.

visible.summary: Mauritania is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous legal environments. The 1983 Penal Code criminalises “acts against nature” with death by stoning (de facto moratorium on executions, but the statute is live); and Cairo 52 documents that gender nonconformity is effectively criminalised through debauchery, heresy, and Islamic-morality provisions — trans people can be apprehended solely for their gender expression. There is no LGR, no healthcare, no community, and sharia courts operate alongside the civil system.
visible.tangentialFactors: “Acts against nature” carries death by stoning (moratorium on executions, statute live) — a catastrophic formal exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents that Mauritania criminalises same-sex sexual activity with a possible death penalty under Sharia law.

Cairo 52 country review: transgender people effectively criminalised through 'debauchery' provisions — Penal Code Art. 264 carries 1 month to 2 years' jail and 5,000-150,000 ouguiya fines for public indecency/debauchery offences applied to gender nonconformity; grave lack of official data on the trans community.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report (Mauritania): consensual same-sex conduct criminalised but penalties not enforced; reports of violence and threats against LGBT people; civil society objected to scant indictments and officials sometimes acted with impunity.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Jan 2026, from Outright): the Penal Code keeps a maximum sentence of death by stoning for men; the government confirmed a de facto death-penalty moratorium in 2021; arrests and detentions under the provisions continue in recent years; low visibility drives stigma; since 2008 the country has served as refuge for Senegulese LGBTIQ people.

Liberals Mauritania (organisation website, c)2026): openly campaigns from within Mauritania on freethinker and LGBT-adjacent causes — titles include 'When the Law Deprives Rights and Freedoms' and 'The First Trans Woman to Speak Out in Mauritania's Media' — evidence of a minimal but real public advocacy space.

visible.summary: Equatorial Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2022 penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct — but a 2024 Synergía report documents twelve women imprisoned between January and August 2024 in police raids led by the Armed Forces and State Security, with detention-for-bribes and indefinite imprisonment; a Draft Law “Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals” (2020, status unclear) would formally criminalise. Africa's longest-ruling dictatorship; no recourse.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2024 raids and the draft criminalisation law target homosexuality — trans people face the same machinery via gender-nonconformity.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 documented prisonings targeted lesbians; trans people face the same machinery via gender-nonconformity.

sources.claim: Synergía IHR report on lesbophobia, human rights and police raids in Equatorial Guinea: police and military intervene in spaces of assembly, expression and residence of lesbian women; in Bata, police detain known lesbians collectively ('lesbians are members of a sect'), including collective punishment when one lesbian is sought.

Outright International profile (updated Mar 2026): the 2022 penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity, but a 2020 Draft Law 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' (status unclear) would effectively criminalise; authorities still apply the obsolete 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which normalises conversion practices and classifies homosexuality as illness; three instruments institutionalise discrimination (Military Justice Code, ministerial order on 'immoral' activities, provincial regulation).
US State Dept 2021 report: same-sex conduct not specifically criminalised but LGBT persons face societal stigma; no anti-discrimination protections, within general repression context.
thin: no usable finding

UPR stakeholder submission (Small Media, EG Justice, IPI, Digital Rights in Equatorial Guinea) for the country's fourth UN review: freedom of expression, digital rights and journalist safety — documents the repressive environment that also constrains LGBT advocacy.

Hispanic Studies Review (Oct 2025): academic analysis of queer motherhood in Equatoguinean novelist Trifonia Melibea Obono's 'Yo no quería ser madre' (2019) — compulsory heterosexuality and queer invisibility as social-climate context.

visible.summary: Eswatini is dangerous for trans visitors. Common law criminalises same-sex intimacy; trans people have no access to LGR and limited healthcare; the absolute monarchy punishes dissent harshly (sedition laws; activists assassinated, per BTI 2024); LGBT people face documented discrimination. Eswatini Pride has proceeded annually since 2018 under heavy conditions — a small space of visibility.
visible.tangentialFactors: Common-law criminalisation of same-sex intimacy — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Monarchy repression is general; Pride proceeds annually.

sources.claim: Country overview updated 12 March 2026: same-sex relations ILLEGAL for men and women throughout Eswatini; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations NOT able to register.
Freedom in the World 2024: Eswatini rated Not Free with an overall score of 17/100 (Political Rights 1/40, Civil Liberties 16/60) - an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space.

BTI 2024 country report: the government denies LGBTQ+ groups the ability to register as organisations, within a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment under an oppressive environment ('Mswati must fall' having become a common protest slogan).

US State Department 2021 report on Eswatini: some traditional, religious and government officials criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In June, LGBTQI+ persons conducted a virtual Pride celebration without incident.
Swazi Media Commentary of December 2018: a church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened - religious-space inclusion documented alongside 'no let-up on discrimination in the kingdom'.

MambaOnline, July 2018: the first eSwatini Pride was declared a 'perfect success' - the inaugural Pride in the kingdom, marking public LGBT visibility in a state where same-sex conduct remains illegal.
MambaOnline, July 2019: Eswatini's registrar of companies refused to register an LGBTI group - the documented administrative blocking of organisational recognition in the kingdom.

visible.summary: Lesotho demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (sodomy common-law crime struck down in 2012); the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho documents failures to prevent violence, harassment and discrimination by state and non-state actors (2024 UPR submission); no LGR; small organised community inside South Africa's geographic envelope.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2012 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: Joint stakeholder UPR report (Oct 2024) by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho on LGBTQ+ rights in Lesotho: documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level SOGIESC discrimination; same-sex conduct is not criminalised but no protections exist.

ICJ UPR submission (Nov 2024) on Lesotho: highlights LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination among three key concerns (alongside inclusive education for children with disabilities and revocation of NGO lawyers' practising certificates).

SALC + People's Matrix Association + WLSA briefing (Oct 2020): 'Legal Gender Recognition in Lesotho' - analysis of law and policy against international best practice; Matrix is the only known LGBTI organisation in Lesotho; researched by Prof Alex Müller with community consultations.

US State Department 2016 Human Rights Report for Lesotho: documents the LDF mutiny arrests, torture of detainees, the killing of Lt-Gen Mahao, and the LGBT section noting no criminalisation but societal stigma.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Lesotho' (2017): constitutional analysis - section 4(1) 'sex' and 'other status' should include gender identity per the UN Human Rights Committee; no law allows gender-marker changes; a trans person using a non-matching passport could be charged; the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omits gender and sexual orientation.

Lesotho Labour Act 2024 (full text, ILO NATLEX): the new labour law - unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, forced and child labour prohibitions - the current statutory framework for workplace rights.
